_comment: BEHAVIOURAL parity pin for token-lint's comment-state tracker (#3337).
token_lint_rules.json makes the four PATTERNS one artifact, and
tokenLintRuleParity.test.ts asserts the TS copies are byte-identical to it. But
deciding which text on a line is CODE is consumer LOGIC, not a pattern — it lives
twice, once per language:
- web/src/design/tokenLintRule.ts  `stripComments`
- personalclaw/apps/quality.py     `strip_comments`
A regex can be shared as data; a lexer cannot. So the BEHAVIOUR is shared as data
instead: every case below is run by BOTH sides' tests, and a case that reds in one
language and passes in the other is a parity break — the same two-dialect defect
the rules file exists to prevent, one layer up.
Each case is a whole synthetic FILE (`lines`), because the defect is cross-line by
nature. `expected` is one entry per line: the violation kinds the rail must report
for that line, in the order hex-then-px. `end_state` is 'code' or 'block' at EOF and
is the load-bearing control: a tracker that leaves block state stuck open reads as
'the rest of the file is clean' and silently stops catching real raw hexes, which
is the ONE way this change could weaken the rail rather than fix it. That is not a
hypothetical: tracking template literals as a third state leaked exactly this way on
three corpus files carrying a backtick inside a regex literal, which is why a backtick
is a LINE-LOCAL quote and only when the line closes it (#3347) — never a state that
can survive a newline. Both halves of that asymmetry are pinned below.
Both directions are represented on purpose. Cases named `red_*` MUST still be
caught (the rail's value); cases named `clean_*` MUST now pass (the bug fixed).
Do not delete a `red_*` case to make a tracker change green — that is the
weakening this file exists to block.
A third prefix, `end_state_*`, pins a file the tracker CANNOT read to the end.
Reporting no line violations is correct for those — the text really is commented
out — so the load-bearing assertion is the 'block' state, which `token_lint_bundle`
turns into a refusal by name (EOF_UNREADABLE) rather than a silent clean verdict.
Two of them are a genuinely broken file; the third is the one shape `strip_comments`
still documents as deliberately unhandled — a `/*` in JSX text whose preceding
character is a SPACE — where failing STRICT is the decision and not an accident.
`end_state` is a NARROW control, and #3347 is the proof: it reports the state the
scan ENDED in, which is not the claim 'the tracker read every line correctly'. A
block that opens wrongly and then CLOSES — a stray `/*` swallowed by the next
unrelated `*/` — ends in 'code', is refused by nothing, and silently drops every
violation in the blanked span. That is why decision 4's look-behind is a fix in the
tracker rather than one more refusal downstream, and why two `red_*` cases here
carry a CLOSED bogus block: nothing else in this file can distinguish the guard
from its absence.

cases.name: clean_interior_line_of_a_multiline_jsx_comment
cases.why: The reported defect. SkillInspector.tsx:65's shape: the issue reference sits on an interior line that carries no comment marker of its own.
lines: {/* Which surface this is: the inspector for a
not the list row — the row only summarises. */}

cases.name: clean_interior_line_of_a_ts_block_comment
cases.why: Same shape in a .ts file with a bare /* … */ rather than JSX braces.
lines: /* Routing note, see #3324 and #532 for the
prior attempts; #1783 is the live one. */

cases.name: clean_jsdoc_continuation_lines
cases.why: A `*`-prefixed continuation line is inside a block, not merely `*`-shaped. The old rule matched the SHAPE; this must hold on state.

cases.name: red_raw_hex_on_a_line_of_real_code
cases.why: Positive control, the base case. If this ever goes clean the rail is worthless.

cases.name: red_raw_hex_on_code_that_FOLLOWS_a_closed_block_comment
cases.why: The specific way a tracker breaks: block state left stuck open after `*/` makes every later line read clean. This case is the one that catches it.

cases.name: red_trailing_code_after_a_block_comment_closed_on_the_SAME_line
cases.why: Edge case, decided deliberately: the comment is stripped and the CODE after it is still linted. Anything else would make `/* … */ const c = '#abc'` a free bypass.

cases.name: red_trailing_block_comment_after_real_code
cases.why: The mirror: code first, comment second. The code half must still red and the comment half must not add a second hit.

cases.name: clean_line_comment_containing_a_block_terminator
cases.why: `app/swPolicy.ts` and `ui/SystemWidget.tsx` shapes: a `//` comment quoting `/*` or `*/`. `//` must win, or the tracker opens a block that never closes.
lines: // the bare comment `/* keep the draft */` cited #1783
// and `*/` alone must not close anything

cases.name: clean_string_literal_containing_a_block_opener
cases.why: `ui/widget/editMode.ts` ships exactly this. A string-unaware tracker treats it as a comment opener and swallows the rest of the file.

cases.name: red_hex_inside_a_string_is_still_a_violation
cases.why: Strings are not comments. Stripping comments must not start excusing string content — that is where every raw colour actually lives.

cases.name: red_hex_inside_a_multiline_template_literal
cases.why: A backtick is only a LINE-LOCAL quote, so it never survives the newline and template CONTENT stays linted across lines: a css-in-template hex is a real violation and the strict direction is to keep catching it.

cases.name: clean_line_comment_inside_an_embedded_js_template
cases.why: `ui/widget/widgetSrcdoc.ts` and `pages/tools/ToolOutput.tsx` ship multi-line templates of embedded JS whose lines start with `//` and cite issue numbers. A line whose first non-space chars are `//` is prose in any non-block state.
lines: // the widget never learns why. Measured twice (#2263), months apart

cases.name: clean_backtick_inside_a_regex_literal_does_not_desync
cases.why: MEASURED: three corpus files carry one — `pages/chat/parseAssistant.ts` (`[\s(`'"]`), `pages/tools/ToolOutput.tsx` and `ui/content/renderers.tsx` (both /^```/m). Tracking template state desynchronised on exactly these and leaked block state to EOF. Telling a regex literal from a division needs real parser context, so a backtick is a line-local quote and only when the line closes it — an unpaired one stays an ordinary character.

cases.name: red_hex_after_a_url_in_jsx_text
cases.why: #3347's first unmodelled shape, pinned on the `://` line itself: a URL in JSX TEXT is not inside a quote, so `//` read as a line comment and truncated the line — a hex sharing that SAME line went unreported with end_state still 'code', invisible to every EOF control. `://` is a scheme separator: only the IMMEDIATELY preceding character counts, so `case 'x': // note` is still prose.

cases.name: red_hex_after_a_protocol_relative_url_in_a_template_literal
cases.why: #3347's second unmodelled shape, the same class one quote-kind over: a template literal is string content, but a backtick was an ordinary character, so `//` inside one truncated the line and hid the hex on it. No colon precedes a protocol-relative `//cdn`, so rule 3 cannot reach this one — the quote set has to.

cases.name: clean_line_comment_after_an_unpaired_backtick_in_a_regex_literal
cases.why: The NEGATIVE control for the case above, and the reason a backtick is a quote only when the line closes it. These three shapes ship today (`renderers.tsx`, `agentFeed.ts`, `scheduleMeta.ts`): one unpaired backtick inside a regex literal, then a real trailing `//` comment citing an issue number. Treating that backtick as a quote would leave the comment linted and re-create #3337, since every decimal digit is a hex digit.
lines: const FENCE = /^```/m,  // fenced code, measured on #1783

cases.name: clean_escaped_quote_does_not_close_the_string
cases.why: A tracker that closes on an escaped quote desynchronises and starts stripping real code as comment.

cases.name: red_nested_jsx_comment_braces_close_at_the_FIRST_terminator
cases.why: JS block comments do not nest, so `{/* {/* */} */}` closes at the first `*/` and the tail is code. Stated rather than assumed: the corpus has no nested shape, and pinning it keeps the two languages from inventing different answers.

cases.name: red_hex_in_a_span_a_stray_block_opener_blanked_and_an_UNRELATED_terminator_closed
cases.why: #3347's live shape, and the one no EOF control can see BECAUSE it closes. `3/*off` opened a block in JSX TEXT, the next ordinary `/* … */` closed it, so end_state came back to 'code', nothing was refused, and the hex two lines inside the blanked span was silently dropped. Positive control for the guard itself: delete the stray and line 3 is caught either way, so this case is the ONLY thing distinguishing the look-behind from its absence. A `/*` whose preceding character is ASCII-alphanumeric or `[` is division or a glob, not an opener.

cases.name: red_hex_after_a_block_opener_inside_a_regex_character_class
cases.why: The same defect one syntax over, and the reason the look-behind admits `[` as well as alphanumerics: in `/[/*]/` the `/*` is two members of a character class. Unquoted, so the string rule cannot help it. It desyncs the tracker exactly like the case above — a later unrelated `*/` closes the bogus block, end_state reads 'code', and the hex on line 2 is lost. NOT the same as clean_backtick_inside_a_regex_literal_does_not_desync, which is backtick desync and not a block opener at all.

cases.name: end_state_block_when_a_comment_never_closes
cases.why: The control's own control. An unterminated `/*` genuinely comments out the rest of the file, so reporting clean lines is CORRECT here — what must not be silent is the state, and `end_state` is how a caller sees it.

cases.name: end_state_block_survives_a_line_comment_it_contains
cases.why: Inside a block, `//` has no meaning. A tracker that honours it there would resume linting mid-comment and re-create the bug one line lower.

cases.name: red_hex_below_a_regex_character_class_that_no_longer_opens_a_block
cases.why: REVERSED from `end_state_block_when_a_regex_character_class_opens_one` (#3378) by the look-behind, and reversed in the STRICTLY STRONGER direction — this is not a weakened assertion. That case declared the right verdict for the tracker as it stood: `/[/*]/` opened a block, nothing closed it, and 'block' at least made `token_lint_bundle` refuse the bundle by name instead of awarding it a badge. But the premise it refused on was never true — the file is valid TypeScript with nothing commented out — so the refusal named the wrong defect and the raw hex on line 2 went unreported. Decision 4 admits `[` as a preceding character, so the class member is no longer an opener, the scan reaches EOF in 'code', and the hex is reported as the line violation it actually is. Loud-but-wrong became loud-and-right; the only thing lost is a false refusal. Still not covered by `clean_backtick_inside_a_regex_literal_does_not_desync`, which is a backtick desync and not a block opener.

cases.name: end_state_block_when_jsx_text_contains_a_wildcard
cases.why:
The shape that is STILL deliberately unhandled (#3347), and the measurement that bounds decision 4's claim: the look-behind admits only an ASCII-alphanumeric or `[` before the `/*`, and here the preceding character is a SPACE, so the block still opens and the file still fails STRICT. So 'a `/*` in JSX text' is not fixed as a category — `

3/*off

` is (see red_hex_in_a_span_…), `

use /* as a wildcard

` is not. Pinned separately from the character-class case for exactly the reason #3378 gave: the two are independently breakable, and the divergence now runs the other way — one is handled and one is not, which is the boundary a future widening must move deliberately rather than by accident. Same STRICT verdict, same reason: a caller must hear that the scan stopped.
